newsitem.title: USA: Tandy to sell Incredible Universe chain.
newsitem.headline: Tandy to sell Incredible Universe chain.

text.p: Tandy Corp. said Monday it plans to sell its Incredible Universe electronics superstores and close 19 Computer City stores, the latest restructuring moves as it attempts to cope with sluggish sales.

Tandy, one of the nation's largest retailers of consumer electronics best known for its Radio Shack stores, said it would take a $170 million charge in the current quarter for the moves, which come amid fierce competition and a slowdown in personal computer sales to consumers.
Industry analysts welcomed the latest steps, which followed an announcement earlier this month that Tandy would shut its remaining McDuff consumer electronics stores because of weak sales.
Tandy officials said they would sell all 17 Incredible Universe stores within six months and close 19 of the 108 Computer City stores in North America and relocate two others.

The Incredible Universe chain was a pet project of Tandy management in the early 1990s but did not perform well. The stores carried a full range of consumer electronics products in large, out-of-the-way locations, but failed to generate sufficient customer traffic or sales.
The stores, which were 150,000 square feet or more, posted losses of almost $40 million in 1995 and were expected to fare worse this year on revenues of about $900 million.

"While individual stores enjoyed success and customers surveyed had strong positives for Incredible Universe, the economic model is not viable for Tandy," Tandy Chairman John Roach said in a statement.
Company officials said the chain was hurt by the intense competition in the consumer electronics industry that has squeezed profit margins and forced higher advertising costs.

The shutdowns will affect more than 4,900 workers but Tandy said it will try to relocate as many of them as possible. An Incredible Universe store employs 250 people on average and each Computer City store has about 35 workers.
"It was a drag not only on profitability but increasingly on shareholder morale," said Peter Caruso at Merrill Lynch, referring to the Incredible Universe chain.
Fort Worth, Tex.-based Tandy has long been viewed as a weak performer in the personal computer business but has been revamping its 6,800 Radio Shack stores and steadily pruning other operations.

The decision to close the 53 remaining McDuff stores, announced on Dec. 10, came after Tandy had closed 49 of the units in January. It had cited a $20 million charge for closing those units, also to be taken in the fourth quarter.

Tandy said it has contracts to sell six Incredible Universe stores to Fry's Electronics Inc., a privately held computer and electronics retailer based in Palo Alto, Calif. Buyers have yet to be found for the other 11 stores.

Under Tandy's restructuring plan, Radio Shack will focus on selling more profitable parts and accessories and use its new telecommunications alliance with Sprint Corp. to sell Internet services, paging products and other goods.
The remaining Computer City stores are to focus more on experienced users, small office and home office customers and the more profitable corporate market.
Tandy officials said the restructuring effort has now been completed.
"Between the McDuff announcement and this one here, this is really the strategy that Tandy wants to take forward," said Martin Moad, vice-president of investor relations.
But analysts said more problems may lie ahead.
"The company is very significantly challenged to turn Computer City around because the external environment is going to be pretty tough for computer retailers in 1997," said Merrill Lynch's Caruso.
